title: The electrical transport of intrinsic two-dimensional ferroelectric metal PtBi2
authors: Dan Li, Liu Yang, Lei Li
abstract: Breaking the conventional stereotype that ferroelectrics are necessarily insulating, two-dimensional (2D) ferroelectric metals combine seemingly incompatible switchable electric polarization and metallic conductivity, providing a fertile ground for the discovery of novel electrical transport phenomena and the development of innovative electronic devices. Using the semiclassical Boltzmann equation and first-principles calculations, we systematically investigate the linear and nonlinear transport responses of the intrinsic 2D ferroelectric metal \ch{PtBi2} to an applied electric field. Our \textit{ab initio} molecular dynamics simulations reveal that it possesses a high Curie temperature reaching $800~\text{K}$. We propose that the crystal structure of its high-temperature paraelectric phase can be explicitly distinguished through simple measurements of the in-plane electrical conductivity. Quantitative calculations of the Edelstein effect and the intrinsic spin Hall effect demonstrate a sizable charge-to-spin conversion efficiency, highlighting its potential in spintronics. We also find that a Berry curvature dipole-induced nonlinear Hall effect emerges in uniaxially strained \ch{PtBi2}. Furthermore, we highlight the unique advantages of 2D ferroelectric metals in gate-controlled transport applications. Based on the domain wall scattering mechanism, we conceptually design a novel ferroelectric metal field-effect transistor (FEM-FET) capable of nonvolatile switching between high-resistance and low-resistance states under a gate voltage. Our work not only unveils the rich transport physics in 2D ferroelectric metals but also provides valuable insights into the design of next-generation nonvolatile memory and spintronic devices.
summary: This work theoretically investigates $	ext{PtBi}_2$, a 2D ferroelectric metal, demonstrating its potential for next-generation electronics. Using first-principles calculations, the authors predict high operational temperatures and significant spin-charge conversion effects. They conclude by proposing a novel nonvolatile memory device concept based on domain wall switching.
main_problem: The study investigates the electrical transport properties of intrinsic two-dimensional (2D) ferroelectric metals, aiming to overcome the limitation that traditional ferroelectrics are often insulating.
main_result: The material exhibits high Curie temperature ($T_C \approx 800\ 	ext{K}$), sizable charge-to-spin conversion efficiencies (Edelstein and SHE), and enables conceptual design of a nonvolatile Ferroelectric Metal Field-Effect Transistor (FEM-FET).
method: The research employs first-principles calculations combined with the semiclassical Boltzmann transport equation to model linear, nonlinear, and spin transport responses.
model_or_system: The physical system is the intrinsic 2D ferroelectric metal $	ext{PtBi}_2$. The theoretical framework involves analyzing its polarization switching, electronic band structure, and resulting charge/spin currents under applied fields.
key_observables: Electrical conductivity ($\sigma_{ab}$), Edelstein effect coefficient ($\chi$), Spin Hall conductivity ($\sigma^{ext}_{i;ab}$), Nonlinear Hall effect (NLHE), and ferroelectric polarization ($P$).
important_parameters: High Curie temperature ($\sim 800\ 	ext{K}$); applied electric field ($E$); uniaxial strain.
main_assumptions: The transport analysis relies on the semiclassical Boltzmann theory, and an effective thickness scaling is used for comparison with bulk materials.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate temperature-dependent polarization confirming high $T_C$, phonon dispersion showing structural phase transitions (FE $\leftrightarrow$ NP), and conductivity anisotropy measurements distinguishing different phases.
paper_structure: The paper systematically analyzes the material's ferroelectric stability via AIMD, calculates linear/nonlinear transport coefficients using Boltzmann theory, discusses spin-related effects (Edelstein/SHE), and culminates in proposing a device concept (FEM-FET) based on domain wall physics.
why_interesting: While focused on condensed matter electronics, the study of polarization switching coupled with charge/spin currents touches upon emergent order parameters and non-equilibrium dynamics that are relevant to advanced quantum control concepts.
